newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Nazi threat forced Swiss to sell arms - diplomat.
newsitem.headline: Nazi threat forced Swiss to sell arms - diplomat.

text.p: A Swiss official responded on Wednesday to revelations his government sold millions of dollars of arms to Adolf Hitler's military in World War Two, saying Nazi Germany's threat was too strong for his small country to resist.

"After 1941, Switzerland was completely surrounded by Nazi Germany and the Axis powers. Therefore my government had to enter into a lot of compromises," said Ambassador Thomas Borer, head of a Swiss Foreign Ministry task force charged with untangling his country's business deals with the Nazis.

Borer spoke hours after the first publication of Swiss diplomatic archives that showed Nazi Germany got the bulk of wartime arms exports from neutral Switzerland, and that the Swiss central bank may have known it was buying looted Nazi gold.
Borer was unsurprised by the revelations.
"It's absolutely known that Switzerland sold arms to Nazi Germany and the Allies. This fact is common knowledge," he said.

Under its neutrality policy during World War Two, Switzerland refrained from supporting either side with armed forces or the use of its territory for military aims. During the war, Switzerland gave refuge to 235,000 refugees and turned away 30,000, according to Swiss government figures.
Borer insisted that Swiss neutrality had not been compromised. "Under neutrality law, you have a right to sell arms to countries in a war," he told a news conference.
But an official of a group that documents the Holocaust said the German threat was no excuse for selling arms to the Nazis.

"I think the Swiss policy of selling arms to the Nazis is basically morally bankrupt. You're talking about selling arms to a totalitarian regime bent on mass annihilation of millions of innocent civilians," said Efraim Zuroff, Director of the Israel office of the Simon Wiesenthal Centre.
Six million Jews died at the hands of Nazi forces.

The diplomatic archives released on Wednesday showed that Swiss arms exports during the war were worth 900 million Swiss francs, and two-thirds of that was sold to the Nazis. Fascist Italy also got 150 million francs worth of arms at a time when the dollar was worth about four Swiss francs.
A report by U.S. Undersecretary of Commerce Stuart Eizenstat has suggested Switzerland may have had $400 million in Nazi gold by the war's end.
The Swiss last year set up a committee to look for dormant assets in Swiss banks, and have set up a $185 million fund to help survivors.

The Swiss president in March proposed a $4.7 billion "Solidarity Foundation" to help victims of humans rights abuses, some of which could aid Holocaust victims. The foundation is subject to voter approval.
Borer said in light of recent revelations about their role in the war, many Swiss feel frustrated by attacks on them.
"They didn't profit from the Second World War, and they had nothing to do with what the Germans did," he said.
